opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The central bet, as I understand it, is that a lot of the most important problems humanity faces, and will face with advanced AI, are fundamentally problems of cooperation rather than problems of individual capability.

When we look at the big failures of human civilization, wars, arms races, the tragedy of the commons with climate change, many of them aren't due to a lack of intelligence on anyone's part. Each actor is often behaving quite reasonably given their circumstances. The failure comes from the structure of the interaction: actors can't credibly commit, can't verify what others are doing, can't communicate their intentions or find mutually beneficial bargains. So you get outcomes that nobody wanted.

The AI field has historically focused on making individual agents more capable, better at solving single-agent problems or winning zero-sum games like chess and Go. The bet behind Cooperative AI is that as we deploy AI systems into the world, we're going to have a world with many AI agents interacting with each other and with many humans and institutions. If we only build up individual capability and neglect cooperative capability, we could end up amplifying exactly the kinds of coordination failures we already struggle with, just faster and at greater scale.

So the program asks: what are the cooperative competencies, things like understanding others, communicating, making and keeping commitments, building and maintaining institutions, and how can AI research help advance them? That includes building AI that is itself better at cooperating, and AI that helps humans cooperate better with each other.

There's an important nuance, though. Cooperative capabilities aren't automatically good. Collusion is a form of cooperation, and cooperation among a subset can come at the expense of others who are excluded. So the bet isn't simply "more cooperation is better." It's that we should deliberately steer toward the kinds of cooperative capabilities that improve social welfare broadly, and that this is a neglected, tractable, and very high-stakes area as AI becomes more central to how the world works.

r001.rationale: The response says Cooperative AI research can advance cooperative capabilities in AI and help humans cooperate, framing this as a neglected, high-stakes area to address cooperation failures.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. I think the central bet is that a lot of the biggest risks from advanced AI aren't really about any single system being misaligned or incompetent. They're about what happens when many capable agents, human and artificial, interact. And the worry is that we could end up in bad equilibria, things like arms races, escalation dynamics, coercion, collusion, collapses of trust, even when every individual actor is behaving roughly rationally and every individual system is doing what its principal wanted.

So the bet is that cooperation is itself a capability, something you can study, measure, and deliberately build into systems and institutions, rather than something that just falls out of making models smarter or more aligned. If you look at what makes humans able to cooperate at scale, it's a mix of things: being able to understand each other, communicate credibly, make and keep commitments, build institutions that structure incentives. None of those come for free. They were hard-won. And there's no guarantee AI systems will develop them in the forms we'd want, or that the environments we deploy them into will reward them.

The second part of the bet is about timing and tractability. Cooperation failures are pretty well understood in game theory and social science, so there's a lot of intellectual machinery to draw on. And we can actually test these things now. You can put language model agents into negotiation settings, into mixed-motive games, and see whether they find mutually beneficial outcomes or whether they defect, deceive, or escalate. That's a real empirical research programme, not just philosophy.

And then the more ambitious hope is that AI could make us better at cooperation than we currently are. If systems can help parties verify each other's claims, design better contracts, find deals that humans couldn't see, then some of the standing coordination problems we have, between companies, between countries, could get easier rather than harder. That's not guaranteed at all. But I think the chance of steering toward that world, rather than the one where AI just supercharges competition, is worth a serious bet.

r001.rationale: The response says cooperation can be deliberately studied and built into AI systems and institutions, and describes how AI could help parties verify claims, design contracts, and find mutually beneficial deals.

astra-6.text:
The central bet is that cooperation is partly a problem of capability. Even when people have good reasons to cooperate, they can fail because they misunderstand one another, can’t find a mutually beneficial agreement, or can’t credibly commit to following through. AI could help us overcome those obstacles.

That’s distinct from making an AI system more altruistic. You can have actors who care primarily about their own interests and still make them all better off by improving their ability to communicate, negotiate, and establish trust. And as AI systems increasingly act on our behalf, we’ll want them to have those abilities themselves.

The important qualification is that cooperation isn’t always socially beneficial. Firms can cooperate to form a cartel; a group can coordinate to harm outsiders. So the aim isn’t simply to maximise cooperation wherever we find it. It’s to understand and develop the capabilities that enable cooperation in ways that support broader human flourishing.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help overcome cooperation problems and that these capabilities should be developed, but it does not clearly identify the bet as investing additional effort now to enable that help.

sol-6.1.text:
The central bet is that making AI systems more capable won’t automatically make them better at cooperating. They might become very good at pursuing their own objectives while still ending up in conflicts that leave everyone worse off. So we should deliberately work on the capabilities that help agents find and achieve mutual gains.

That includes understanding what others want, communicating, making credible commitments, and finding arrangements that people have reason to trust. The hope is that progress on those problems could help both AI systems cooperate with one another and humans cooperate with each other.

But cooperation isn’t automatically good. A cartel is cooperating. So the aim isn’t just to make any group better at coordinating; it’s to enable cooperation that benefits people broadly, including those who aren’t represented at the negotiating table.

r001.rationale: It says we should deliberately work on cooperation capabilities and that progress could help AI systems cooperate, clearly expressing that investment can help address cooperation problems.
